title: Cîteaux (1098)
hook: monks seek a simpler, stricter Benedictine life in white habits

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anselm, the monk who called his book faith seeking understanding. What honest question did you ask? Today, monks who decided they wanted less. Day eight hundred one.

An iron candlestick. A cross of painted wood, not gold. Walls of bare stone, and light coming in through plain glass. Stand in an old Cistercian church and the first thing you may notice is what isn't there. No crowd of carved monsters on the columns. No silver on the altar. Just stone, light, and the sound of a few voices singing psalms. The builders chose less, on purpose. Today's word is the name of the monks who chose it: Cistercian.
screen: `AN IRON CANDLESTICK.` → `WHAT ISN'T THERE.` → `LESS, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Start with the leaving. Robert, abbot of a monastery called Molesme, came to think that he and his monks weren't keeping the Rule of Saint Benedict as it was written. So he left, with a group of brothers, and founded what the early accounts simply call the New Monastery, in a wild, lonely place called Cîteaux. Next, what they cut. Their own early account says they set aside whatever they couldn't find in the Rule: fur garments, undershirts, extra dishes at table. They went back to working the land with their own hands. They wore habits of undyed wool, which is why people came to call them the white monks. Then, the churches. Early Cistercian rules ask for crosses of painted wood, not gold or silver, and candlesticks of iron. The aim wasn't ugliness. It was attention: nothing in the room competing with prayer. Finally, the bond. One of the early abbots, Stephen Harding, is credited with a Charter of Charity linking the new houses, so they kept one way of life and looked after one another. Cluny and Cîteaux both followed Benedict, and the Church honors saints from each; they heard the same Rule in different keys. Jesus says to Martha, in the Douay-Rheims: "thou art careful, and art troubled about many things: But one thing is necessary." Some readers hear the whole Cistercian plan in that sentence. That's today's line: plainer.
screen: `LEAVING FOR THE NEW MONASTERY.` · `CUT WHAT ISN'T IN THE RULE.` · `PAINTED WOOD, IRON, PLAIN GLASS.` · `A CHARTER OF CHARITY.` · then, large: `PLAINER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: simplify one thing. For the sit, look around the room you're in, or walk through your day in your mind. Find one thing that crowds out what matters: a cluttered corner, an app you open without meaning to, a commitment you keep out of habit. Don't fix it yet. Just see it plainly, and let yourself feel the space it would leave. If you pray, you can rest in Jesus's words to Martha: one thing is necessary. After the bell, take one small step: clear the corner, move the app, let one thing go. The bell holds the time.
Cistercian. A monk or nun of the way of life born at Cîteaux: the Rule of Benedict kept closely, in undyed wool, with plain churches and work of the hands. Today's word.
Your line: plainer. Today, when you're about to add one more thing, pause and ask whether one less would do. Then choose. Day eight hundred one.

howItsDone: Cistercian monks and nuns, including the Trappists, still live by the Rule of Saint Benedict with manual work, silence and the hours of prayer, and their abbey churches are kept plain; some abbeys welcome guests for retreats.

fork.setup: you're a monk in a comfortable, respected monastery, but you think the Rule is being softened. what do you do?
options: leave with a few brothers to start a plainer house in a wild place.
fork.reveal: Robert of Molesme left with a group of monks and founded the New Monastery at Cîteaux to keep the Rule more closely.

trapdoor: what you thought: Cistercian is just a fancy word for a monk.
what it means: a monk or nun of the way of life born at Cîteaux, keeping the Rule of Benedict in a plainer, stricter form.
what a scholar hears: the early Cîteaux documents: no fur or fine linen, painted wooden crosses, iron candlesticks, a Charter of Charity.

notes: Exordium Parvum paraphrased: Robert of Molesme and brothers leave to keep the Rule more purely; the 'New Monastery'; rejection of what is not in the Rule (cowls of fur, shirts, extra dishes, etc.); manual labor. Confirm items listed.
Painted wooden crosses and iron candlesticks: from early Cistercian statutes (often cited from the Exordium Parvum ch. 17 / Instituta). Confirm source and wording.
'The white monks' for undyed habits: general; confirm.
Carta Caritatis attributed to Stephen Harding; the dates in the title and the annual general chapter are left unvoiced under the claims rule.

Cluny and Cîteaux framed as two ways of hearing the same Rule, without ranking; Bernard's Apologia critique of ornament (carved monsters) is alluded to in the hook only as 'no crowd of carved monsters on the columns'. Confirm fairness.

Editor pass: 'marshy' (etymology lore) changed to 'lonely'; 'fine shirts' to 'undershirts'; cut the unsupported 'couldn't afford more' line (early Cîteaux was poor); Charter of Charity now 'credited with'; 'built whole monasteries around that sentence' softened to 'some readers hear'.
Audit pass (days 797-806): read in full; Douay-Rheims quotations and source paraphrases checked; no change needed.
